prompt.context: Your client, Texas Oil, is a large, integrated oil and gas company which competes with the likes of ExxonMobil, Shell, and Chevron. They have assets in 72 countries, on 5 continents, and own one-quarter of the US oil market. They recently purchased a large area of land from a small, independent oil company and are attempting to integrate it into their portfolio in West Texas. They hired your firm to help them determine how to develop the purchased land. While the company is large, it is "capital constrained". This is because of low crude oil prices and an over-budget refinery in Angola. As a result, the company cannot develop all of the purchased land in the coming years.
prompt.question: How would you frame this problem for the client? How many acres can Texas Oil develop before their lease expires, and what percentage of their purchased land does this represent? How should Texas Oil prioritize and develop its purchased land given its capital constraints?

clarifying_info.q: Do all of the purchased land areas have confirmed oil and gas reserves?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, all of the purchased land has proven oil and gas reserves (with 90% confidence).

clarifying_info.q: Are other competitors active in West Texas?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, other major competitors are also in West Texas.

clarifying_info.q: Does the quality of reserves matter (oil vs. gas)?
clarifying_info.a: Oil and gas are commodities traded on an international, liquid market, so the quality of the reserves is not important for this case.

clarifying_info.q: Can Texas Oil influence the price of oil or gas?
clarifying_info.a: No, Texas Oil does not have enough market share to influence the price of oil or gas.

clarifying_info.q: How long is left on the lease?
clarifying_info.a: The purchased lease will expire in 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: How much land was purchased in total?
clarifying_info.a: The total amount purchased is 320,000 acres.

clarifying_info.q: How much capital is available for development?
clarifying_info.a: The company has $300 million available to spend.

clarifying_info.q: What is the company's primary objective — profit or production?
clarifying_info.a: The company wants to maximize profitability given its capital constraints.

framework: Frame as a prioritization problem: Texas Oil cannot develop all purchased land before the lease expires in 3 years, so it must select which focus areas to develop first.

Cost-benefit analysis to evaluate each focus area: Costs include land development (roads, infrastructure), appraisal (geological analysis), construction and drilling, labor, and production (pipelines). Benefits include revenue, market share, and production volumes.
Capital constraint: Total available capital is $300MM, so the combination of developed focus areas must not exceed this budget.
Lease expiration risk: Only land developed within 3 years generates value; undeveloped land at lease expiry is forfeited.
Prioritization criteria: NPV maximization, capital efficiency (NPV per dollar of cost), total cost within budget, and optionally total production volume.

questions.prompt: How many acres can Texas Oil develop before their lease expires, and what percentage of their purchased land does this represent?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for the development rate and unit conversion, then calculate: (rate in sq miles/year) x (years remaining) x (acres per sq mile). Strong candidates set up the math clearly and check units.

math.setup: Development rate = 100 square miles/year; lease remaining = 3 years; 1 square mile = 640 acres; total purchased = 320,000 acres
steps: Square miles developable = 100 sq miles/year x 3 years = 300 square miles
Acres developable = 300 sq miles x 640 acres/sq mile = 192,000 acres
math.answer: Texas Oil can develop 192,000 acres, which is 60% of its purchased land.

questions.prompt: How would you prioritize the five focus areas? What factors would you consider?
questions.guidance: NPV is the base answer. Strong candidates go further: (1) capital efficiency — some areas may have higher absolute NPV but cost more to develop, making them less attractive when capital is scarce; (2) total cost — must stay within $300MM capital budget; (3) total production — some companies are production-focused because it boosts stock price or company valuation (relevant for independents looking to sell, less so here). Candidate should distinguish between maximizing total NPV and maximizing NPV per dollar spent.

questions.prompt: Given Exhibit 2 (Focus Area Figures) and Exhibit 3 (Capital Efficiencies) and a $300MM capital budget, how should Texas Oil develop its purchased land?
questions.guidance: The key metric is capital efficiency. The correct combination is Eagle Mountain + Midland + Fox Path. Total cost = $94MM + $96MM + $108MM = $298MM (within $300MM budget). Total NPV = $45MM + $45MM + $50MM = $140MM. Coyote Tooth can substitute for Fox Path (same NPV of $50MM) but costs $110MM vs $108MM — slightly less capital efficient. Nag River Head has the highest individual NPV ($55MM) but costs $150MM; pairing it with any two other areas exceeds $300MM, forcing the company to drop a third area and forfeit that NPV. Nag River Head is not capital efficient. Second-level insights: Texas Oil could re-categorize land within segments to achieve higher portfolio efficiencies (not all land in one segment is equally profitable); Texas Oil should sell excess acreage to competitors rather than letting the lease expire.

math.setup: Capital budget = $300MM. Evaluate all combinations of 3 focus areas (since 60% of land = 3 out of 5 areas at 64,000 acres each). Compare total cost and total NPV for each combination.
steps: Eagle Mountain + Midland + Fox Path: Cost = $94 + $96 + $108 = $298MM (under $300MM); NPV = $45 + $45 + $50 = $140MM
Eagle Mountain + Midland + Coyote Tooth: Cost = $94 + $96 + $110 = $300MM (at limit); NPV = $45 + $45 + $50 = $140MM
Eagle Mountain + Midland + Nag River Head: Cost = $94 + $96 + $150 = $340MM — EXCEEDS $300MM budget
Eagle Mountain + Fox Path + Nag River Head: Cost = $94 + $108 + $150 = $352MM — EXCEEDS $300MM
Midland + Fox Path + Nag River Head: Cost = $96 + $108 + $150 = $354MM — EXCEEDS $300MM
Any combination including Nag River Head violates the $300MM cap when paired with two other areas

Capital efficiency check: Eagle Mountain NPV/Cost = 45/94 = 47.9%; Fox Path = 50/108 = 46.3%; Midland = 45/96 = 46.9%; Coyote Tooth = 50/110 = 45.5%; Nag River Head = 55/150 = 36.7% — lowest efficiency
math.answer: Optimal selection: Eagle Mountain, Midland, and Fox Path. Total cost $298MM, total NPV $140MM. Nag River Head is excluded despite highest individual NPV because it is the least capital efficient and causes any three-area combination to exceed the $300MM budget.

brainstorming.prompt: How would you go about prioritizing the five focus areas beyond a simple NPV comparison?

categories.name: Financial metrics
ideas: NPV of each focus area (revenue from reserves minus development costs)
Capital efficiency (NPV per dollar of total cost)

categories.name: Capital constraint considerations
ideas: Total cost of development must fit within $300MM budget
Combination of areas that maximizes NPV within budget
Avoid areas that are capital-intensive relative to their returns

categories.name: Production and strategic value
ideas: Total production volume (barrels of oil equivalent) — can boost stock price and company valuation
Production mix (oil vs. gas vs. NGLs) and commodity price outlook
Strategic fit with existing West Texas assets and infrastructure

categories.name: Operational factors
ideas: Ease of land development (roads, infrastructure already in place)
Proximity to existing pipelines and processing facilities

categories.name: Portfolio optimization
ideas: Re-categorize land within focus areas to select only the highest-value sub-parcels
Sell or sublease excess acreage to competitors rather than forfeiting to lease expiry
Sequence development to preserve optionality on remaining areas

recommendation: Texas Oil should develop Eagle Mountain, Midland, and Fox Path — the three focus areas that maximize NPV ($140MM combined) while staying within the $300MM capital budget (total cost $298MM).

Nag River Head, despite the highest individual NPV ($55MM), should not be developed in this cycle because it is the least capital efficient (36.7% NPV/Cost ratio) and its inclusion in any three-area combination exceeds the $300MM capital constraint.
risks: Oil and gas commodity prices may decline further, reducing revenue projections for all areas.
Development costs may overrun estimates, particularly if the company is already over budget on the Angola refinery.
Lease expiry in 3 years creates execution risk if development pace slows.
Competitors in West Texas may acquire the acreage Texas Oil forfeits at lease expiry.
next_steps: Sell or sublease the two undeveloped focus areas (Nag River Head and Coyote Tooth) to competitors before the lease expires to capture residual value.
Review land parcels within Eagle Mountain, Midland, and Fox Path to re-categorize and prioritize the highest-value sub-segments first.
Monitor capital budget throughout development; if costs underrun on early areas, revisit developing Coyote Tooth with remaining capital.
Evaluate options to extend the lease or negotiate with landowner if development pace falls behind.
